body: Step 1's Currency check (Implementation §3 point 5) drops a target "unless it is present in the caller's current `declared_step_ids` *and* `step_statuses.get(target) is not StepStatus.DONE`." When `target` is a key missing from `step_statuses`, `.get(target)` returns `None`, and `None is not StepStatus.DONE` is `True` — the check silently passes as if the step were confirmed not-done, contradicting the plan's own stated principle in the same Architecture point 6 ("never guess a target and never pass an unresolved or stale one through"). Step 4's real wiring always builds `step_statuses` over every step in the plan so this can't happen in production, but step 1's classifier is a standalone function with `declared_step_ids` and `step_statuses` documented as "two independent parameters" and tested with independent fixture data — nothing in the plan states what a target-in-`declared_step_ids`-but-absent-from-`step_statuses` case should do, and step 1's own test roster has no case for it (only a case for a present, `DONE` status).
suggested_action: state in the Currency rule that a target present in `declared_step_ids` but absent as a key in `step_statuses` counts as unresolved status and must be dropped, not treated as not-done, and add a test for that case to step 1's roster alongside the existing done-status test.

body:
Step 5's structural proof that no accepted-head write escapes the guarded swap has no stated scope, and the two natural readings require very different tests. Testing says:

  ```
  prove by a test over the write call graph
  that the only site ever writing `accepted_head_path` is the guarded,
  journaled selector swap
  ```

  At HEAD, several paths already write that file:
  - Root enrollment creates the head rather than swapping it (`roadmap_versions.py:build_root_enrollment_generation`).
  - `promote_review_seal` swaps it.
  - `recover_roadmap_publication`'s un-enrolled branch restores recorded old bytes for every generation member (`_replace_generation_members`).

Both readings satisfy the acceptance criterion "the accepted-head-write boundary is proven structurally" and step 5's intent ("without any accepted-head write path outside the guarded selector swap").
suggested_action: State the proof's scope: for example, "settlement's modules write the accepted head only through a `PendingGeneration` published by `publish_roadmap_generation`". Name the existing writers it deliberately does not cover, in Testing, the acceptance criterion, and step 5's intent.

body:

The Architecture also says bundling the version files with the selector swap "removes the interrupted-between-the-two-writes case entirely". Root enrollment escapes this because its selector is written last and a missing head falls back to the un-enrolled rollback path. After the roadmap's one candidate admission is used, nothing else can cure it either, because `roadmap_candidate_run.py:run_initial_candidate_proposal` refuses any other feedback selector, before and after promotion.
  Affected sites: the Architecture "Enrolled roadmap" bullet, step 5, step 7, the acceptance criterion quoted below, and Testing cases 12 and 14.
  ```
  `ROADMAP_FORMAT.md` and `docs/how-to/roadmap.md` state all three enrolled settlement limits, each with its backlog pointer
  ```
suggested_action: Correct the claim that bundling "removes the case entirely". title: The ledger lifecycle does not define how a `closed` or `deferred` item re-enters eligibility. Architecture explicitly ma
body:
The ledger lifecycle does not define how a `closed` or `deferred` item re-enters eligibility. Architecture explicitly makes an awaiting-review reopen become `open`, while Testing and acceptance criteria promise that a closed item can reopen or retarget; implementers can reasonably leave a reopened closed/deferred item in its old ineligible state or make it open.

```text
Architecture: “Reopening an `awaiting-review` item, or editing its request or target, clears its live proposal fields and makes it `open`.”

Architecture: “a closed item keeps its stable id and current fields, is never eligible, and may later be reopened or retargeted as that same mutable item.”
```

This spans Architecture, Testing, Acceptance criteria, step 1 (`Define the canonical mutable feedback ledger, target fingerprints, and eligibility rules`), and step 6 (`Add explicit idempotent legacy migration and guarded mutable reviewer edits in predecessor-grouped ledger sections`).
suggested_action: Define the resulting state and proposal-field effects for reopening or editing every retained ineligible state, and use that one lifecycle rule across the ledger, reviewer-edit commands, tests, and acceptance criteria.

title: The ledger lifecycle leaves the meaning of an `awaiting-review` item open after a reviewer reopens or retargets it. Arch
body: The ledger lifecycle leaves the meaning of an `awaiting-review` item open after a reviewer reopens or retargets it. Architecture says both that “every admitted item moves from `open` to `awaiting-review`, records its proposed response, and records the immutable candidate revision id that produced it” and that “Later reviewer edits may reopen, close, retarget, or replace the current ledger fields”; Testing also requires reopening an awaiting-review item. Steps 1 (`Define the canonical mutable feedback ledger, target fingerprints, and eligibility rules`), 4 (`Build feedback-free successor artifacts and a response patch limited to the admitted batch`), 6 (`Add explicit idempotent legacy migration and guarded mutable reviewer edits in predecessor-grouped ledger sections`), and 8 (`Bind candidate questions, answers, rejection, and discard resolution to the exact active-candidate batch`) do not say whether reopen/retarget clears or retains the prior response and candidate provenance, or whether it changes the active candidate’s review status. Implementers can therefore either present an old proposal as the response for a newly targeted item or silently discard its current-ledger link while both preserve immutable evidence.
suggested_action: Define the state and proposal-field effects of reopen, retarget, close, rejection, and discard for awaiting-review items, and reconcile the ledger, candidate-review, and lifecycle tests to that rule.

body:

  Settlement also refuses while the roadmap's one admitted, unpromoted
    candidate lineage's predecessor is the current accepted head
  ```

suggested_action: Either state the permanent block as an accepted limit (in step 5's refusal wording, a step 8 doc line, the acceptance criterion, and a backlog entry), or define which lineage states still allow settlement. Do not leave it implicit.

body: The Overview states closed feedback rows "are retained in the `feedback` collection (never deleted)," but step 3's title commits to "keep the reviewer's delete-the-row close working" — the very mechanism the Problem statement blames for today's loss ("A reviewer resolves a row only by deleting it before a run"). body: The checkpoint's write-time verification (step 2) is wired only into `_run_roadmap`'s stage-run path, but `seed-state.json` — one of the ten tracked inventory files — is also written by three other roadmap actions dispatched straight from `cmd_roadmap` before the stage-run code ever runs: `refresh_roadmap_seeds` (`--refresh-seeds`), `_accept_roadmap_seed` (`--accept-seed`), and `apply_roadmap_seeds` (`--apply`), each calling `_write_roadmap_seed_state` directly. None of these three actions appears in the plan's Scope guardrails' "No change to `--revise-feedback`, `--materialize`, `--enroll-baselines`, or `--enroll-version`" list, and the plan's Risk section frames the "another writer's change" hazard only as "a later hand edit" or something "outside this tool's own generation history" — it never considers an ordinary, same-tool seed action running between two attempts of the same failed revision. Nothing appears to be actually broken here: the whole-vector bytes comparison in step 3's restore matrix, and the write-time check in step 2, would both treat the seed action's change to `seed-state.json` the same as any other unexpected change and refuse rather than silently overwrite it. But that refusal also discards the legitimate `--refresh-seeds`/`--accept-seed`/`--apply` work along with the failed run's own restore/retry, and no test in either step 2's or step 3's roster exercises this specific, plausible-in-practice sequence (retry a failed roadmap revision, or restore it, after running one of these three seed actions).
suggested_action: Name `--refresh-seeds`, `--accept-seed`, and `--apply` as legitimate other writers of the tracked `seed-state.json` file in the plan's Risk section, and add one test (to step 2's or step 3's roster) proving that a seed action's write between two runs of the same checkpoint lineage is caught by the existing mismatch check and refuses safely rather than being folded into the next write.

title: The Testing section lists refusal cases as one semicolon-separated set:
body:
The Testing section lists refusal cases as one semicolon-separated set:
  ```
  Cover every refusal class as its own case: missing or mismatched
  decision target; an inherited decision selected as target; a
  non-pending decision (already settled); missing, mismatched, or
  empty-response feedback evidence; a changed source baseline between
  evidence selection and confirmation; an in-flight pending generation
  (enrolled only); and an attempt to write an accepted head directly
  (enrolled only).
  ```
  That is seven distinct cases, but the Acceptance criteria section says
  ```
  Each of the six refusal classes above stops the action before any
  publication, with a distinct, named reason.
  ```
  A reader can't tell whether "six" is a plain miscount (all seven need their own named reason, matching step 2's own "one named refusal per rejection class") or whether two of the seven are meant to share one refusal reason — and if so, which two. The most likely candidates to collapse, the two enrolled-only cases ("in-flight pending generation" and "write the accepted head directly"), are materially different failure conditions (one is a leftover journal, the other is a route trying to bypass the candidate/promotion path entirely), so folding them into one shared name would itself violate step 2's "one named refusal per rejection class" requirement. Left as written, a test author following the acceptance bar's literal count could stop one refusal case short of the coverage the Testing section already commits to.
suggested_action: Correct the acceptance criterion's count to match the seven distinct cases the Testing section lists, or state explicitly which two cases are intended to share a single named refusal reason and why, so the acceptance bar and the test list agree on how many distinct, named refusal reasons the route must produce.

```

title: Steps 3 (settlement receipt record), 4 and 5 never say whether the settlement receipt is committed to git, and the two p
body:
Steps 3 (settlement receipt record), 4 and 5 never say whether the settlement receipt is committed to git, and the two precedents the plan names do opposite things. Architecture "Receipt" says:

  ```
  publishes one durable, immutable, create-once record — following the
  existing immutable-evidence pattern already used for escalation and
  impact-analysis receipts, not a new ad hoc log — naming the artifact key,
  ```

  - **Escalation receipts:** `roadmap_escalation_run.py` stores the final and then commits only that file to `HEAD` through `cli/gitcommit.py:commit_receipt`. `ROADMAP_FORMAT.md` trusts an escalation receipt only after that commit, with `created`, `reused` and `committed-existing` versus `commit-failed` and `collision` outcomes.
  - **Impact analyses:** stay local. `.gitignore` excludes `**/.plan-tool/evidence/impact-analyses/` as "local runtime evidence".

  Each reading changes what the command does:
  - **Committed:** settlement makes a git commit holding only the receipt, while the settled artifact stays an uncommitted working-tree change. It also needs commit-failure and collision outcomes the plan never lists.
  - **Local and ignored:** the receipt never travels with the artifact ("Artifacts are committed docs"), so the after-the-fact proof exists only on the machine that ran the settlement.
  - **Neither:** the new namespace shows up as untracked files.

  Sites: Architecture "Receipt" bullet; step 3 (new namespace in `roadmap_evidence_store.py`); steps 4 and 5; step 8's docs; the receipt acceptance criterion.
suggested_action: State whether the settlement receipt is committed to `HEAD` (the escalation shape, with its commit outcomes) or kept as ignored local evidence (the impact-analysis shape). Assign the chosen git or `.gitignore` behavior to its owning step, and have step 8 and the receipt acceptance criterion reflect it.

body:

title: A stack rooted at a settlement-published head has no test owner. Steps 1 and 3 hand the assertion to step 7, and step 7
body:
A stack rooted at a settlement-published head has no test owner. Steps 1 and 3 hand the assertion to step 7, and step 7 has no such case. The plan requires it in its Acceptance criteria, and Testing repeats the same list ("each asserted as a carve-out"):

  ```
  Legacy candidates without a route or without a recorded root, all-presentation stacks, and stacks rooted at an enrolled root, a previously promoted structural candidate, or a settlement-published head keep their current routes.
  ```

  Step 1's Deferred list and step 3's Deferred list each say `including a stack rooted at a settlement-published head — step 7 owns them`. Step 7's route table, test list, and carve-out bullet cover only route-less candidates, all-presentation stacks, and selector-era candidates. The root tests that do exist use other roots: step 1's `test_the_root_hops_own_structural_route_is_never_counted` (a promoted structural candidate, which has candidate evidence), step 1's other fixtures (the enrolled root), and step 3's `test_a_stack_rooted_at_a_promoted_structural_candidate_does_not_count_the_roots_route`. A settlement head is a different kind of root. `plan_tool/roadmap_decision_settlement_enrolled.py` publishes it with `create_candidate_version`, so it is a `candidate`-kind version, and it writes no candidate evidence. The design already handles it, because the walk ends at the recorded root by id and `source_ancestry_to_root` never loads the root. This is a missing owner for the test, not a design gap.
suggested_action: Either give one step the settlement-head-root case (a candidate-kind root with no evidence leaves the stack derivable) and repoint the two Deferred lines at that step. Or drop "a settlement-published head" from the plan's Testing and Acceptance lists and from those two Deferred lines, saying the enrolled-root and promoted-candidate cases cover the same two root properties.

title: Step 5 (enrolled settlement) picks a no-review sentinel for `review_lineage_identity` but says nothing about `content_id
body:
Step 5 (enrolled settlement) picks a no-review sentinel for `review_lineage_identity` but says nothing about `content_identity`, the other identity field that `create_candidate_version` requires to be non-null. The only existing value for that field is a model-candidate digest, so the plan's "nothing needs to be faked" claim has a hole. Risks "Synthetic provenance" says:

  ```
  reviewer-sealed. The dedicated settlement sentinel and `PendingGeneration`
  kind exist precisely so nothing needs to be faked.
  ```

  At HEAD, `roadmap_versions.py:StoredRoadmapVersion` rejects a candidate with any null binding (`predecessor_version_id`, `content_identity`, `review_lineage_identity`). The only producer of `content_identity`, `roadmap_candidate.py:_content_identity`, hashes the selected feedback, the model capsule `receipt`, and a `predecessor_diff`. An implementer must either build a fake capsule receipt to reuse that function, which is the synthetic provenance the Risk forbids, or invent a meaning the plan never states. The Testing section checks only the sentinel. The stored version record is the one lasting link between an accepted head and what produced it, so `content_identity` is also the natural place for a settlement version to name its receipt. Sites: Architecture "Enrolled roadmap" bullet, step 5 title, Risks "Synthetic provenance", and the Testing sentence on `review_lineage_identity`.
suggested_action: State that a settlement version's `content_identity` is a settlement-owned identity, for example one computed over the predecessor version id, artifact key, decision id, and cited feedback id/digest, or the receipt's identity. It must never come from `roadmap_candidate._content_identity` or a synthetic capsule receipt. Add it to the Testing assertion next to the sentinel.

The first acceptance criterion promises enrolled settlement whenever the candidate lineage is not permanently stalled. But the refusal it summarizes blocks every admitted, unpromoted lineage on the current head, including one that will later be promoted. The criterion ends:

  whose one candidate lineage (if any) is not permanently stalled on the

A test written from the criterion expects settlement to succeed while a lineage is still in progress; a test written from case 12 expects a refusal.

title: The Architecture gives incompatible no-work rules: it first returns no-work whenever there are no eligible reviewer item
body:
The Architecture gives incompatible no-work rules: it first returns no-work whenever there are no eligible reviewer items, but later permits a derived-context-only run. Steps 3 (`Build one ordered root-and-active-candidate batch from eligible reviewer feedback and current roadmap-derived context`) and 10 (`Route selector-free feedback commands to the ledger lifecycle`) could therefore either skip or create a candidate when only nondeleted roadmap-derived context exists; Testing and Acceptance criteria select the latter rule.

Architecture: “Selector-free `--revise-feedback` returns deterministic `no-work` without a backend call or write when zero eligible reviewer-created `open` items exist”
```

```

title: Step 2 (settlement preflight) must accept "one live `feedback` row" as evidence, but the plan never says which `Feedback
body:
Step 2 (settlement preflight) must accept "one live `feedback` row" as evidence, but the plan never says which `FeedbackState`s count. The precedent it tells step 2 to follow refuses the very row its motivating case produces. Architecture "Evidence is a binary fact" says:

  ```
  selector naming one live `feedback` row in the same artifact whose
  `request` field — "the reviewer's own words," per `FeedbackRow`'s own
  docstring, and never rewritten by the model — is non-empty and targets the
  decision,
  ```

  At HEAD, every feedback selector refuses anything but an untouched `open` row. `roadmap_escalation_selection.py:select_receipt_feedback` returns `not-open` and `already-responded`, and `roadmap_revision.py:preflight_feedback_revision` requires `FeedbackState.OPEN` with no `proposed_response`. The References section names `roadmap_escalation_selection.py` as the precedent for the refusal shape. But the case this plan exists to close is an approval recorded through ordinary review (`--revise-feedback` or a stage-feedback revision), and `roadmap_revision_patch.py` leaves that row `awaiting-review` with a `proposed_response`. So one implementer copies the precedent and refuses the motivating case, while another accepts any row in the file, including a `deferred` row the reviewer parked. The feedback lifecycle in `ROADMAP_FORMAT.md` also defines closing a row as deleting it. An operator who accepts the response first therefore deletes the only evidence the route accepts, and no step tells them to settle first. Sites: Architecture "Evidence is a binary fact" and "Feedback disposition" bullets, the Scope guardrails bullet on "a named, live feedback row", step 2 intent, the References `roadmap_escalation_selection.py` bullet, the Testing refusal list, acceptance criterion 1, and step 8 (document the settlement route).
suggested_action: Decide once which feedback states count as evidence (for example, any row present in the artifact, or only `open` and `awaiting-review`). If answered rows qualify, say that the precedent's `not-open`/`already-responded` checks are deliberately not carried over. Add an ineligible-state refusal to the Testing list, and have step 8 tell operators to settle before closing (deleting) the evidence row.

title: Step 4's un-enrolled write marks every tracked derived seed invalidated, but no step documents that settlement has this
body:

body:
Testing and the acceptance criteria assert the output carve-outs for selector-era candidates and single-hop presentation-only proposals, but not three other exclusions the plan states on purpose. A change that adds the stack or a confirm step to these surfaces keeps every listed test green.
  - Step 6 (`Render step 4's shared stack printout on the proposal output ...`) says "standalone --reject-candidate and --discard-candidate output is unchanged". Scope guardrails says the same exclusion is Not allowed:

  ```

    reviewer `request` text, and passing the required confirm flag — with no
    hand-edit of any artifact file, on both an un-enrolled and an enrolled

The plan defines a hop by stored `CandidateProposalEvidence` (Architecture "Stack route": "reads the stored `CandidateProposalEvidence.operation_classification`"; step 1). It says "Answered replacements and legacy evidence that has no route keep their current behavior", but never says how an answered replacement appears as a hop.   - It has no `operation_classification` and no batch receipt with `reviewer_items`.
  - It is stored as `candidate-review-replacement.json`, so `load_stored_candidate_proposal` cannot load it.

  - Step 6 renders the stack on the answered route's answer output and on `--promote-review-seal`. On the answered route the promoted head is the replacement, which takes the place of the reviewed candidate and shares its source.
  - Criterion 4 says the promote output "lists the same hops after the head has moved".

  It is unclear whether the answered route lists the reviewed initial candidate or its replacement as the top hop. It is also unclear what that hop shows for "stored route" and "selected feedback", which its own evidence lacks. The review and answer surfaces could list the initial candidate while the promote surface lists the replacement, so the hops differ and the criterion fails. Or the two surfaces could show different route and feedback facts for the same hop.
  Affected: Architecture "Stack route" and "Stack view"; step 1; step 4; step 6; acceptance criterion 4.

State what that hop shows for route and selected feedback, since its own evidence stores no route. title: Step 5 (enrolled settlement) never says whether the settlement version's stored files are written in the same journaled
body:
Step 5 (enrolled settlement) never says whether the settlement version's stored files are written in the same journaled write as the accepted-head swap. The two descriptions it gives point different ways. Architecture "Enrolled roadmap" says:

  ```
  Settlement stores its settled artifact bytes as an ordinary
  `version_kind: "candidate"` record via the existing
  `create_candidate_version` (`roadmap_versions.py`)
  ```

  and:

  ```
  `accepted_head_path` advances under the existing writer-token lease and
  `PendingGeneration` journal — the same selector-swap mechanics
  `promote_review_seal` uses, under one new, additive
  `PendingGeneration.kind` value (e.g. `"decision-settlement"`) recognized
  by the recovery function's existing kind-branch alongside
  `"root-enrollment"`
  ```

  **What HEAD does today:**
  - `create_candidate_version` only builds a record. The candidate pipeline writes version files through its own `candidate-proposal` generation (`roadmap_candidate_run.py:_store_candidate`).
  - `promote_review_seal`'s generation holds only the selector. `_is_completed_version_owned_generation` accepts `review-seal-promotion` only with exactly one member, while `root-enrollment` holds the version files plus the selector.

  **Why the gap matters.** Suppose the files are written first, in a separate write, and the process is interrupted before the head moves. A retry builds the same version id, because settlement is deterministic. Under "stored version members are never overwritten or deleted", the plan gives that retry no outcome: reuse or permanent refusal. This case also falls outside any journal that the deferred "Incomplete immutable lifecycle journals" entry covers. That undercuts the Architecture "Receipt" goal that a retry after an interrupted first attempt can finish.
suggested_action: State whether the settlement version's stored files and the head swap are one journaled generation (as root enrollment is) or two writes. If two, say what a retry does when it finds its own identical version already stored. Carry the choice into step 5's title and into step 8's journals BUG_BACKLOG.md extension.

body:
The plan gives two opposite fixes for evidence that sits in a non-canonical artifact. Step 7's docs and the case-9 refusal can only tell the operator one of them. The Architecture section's "Un-enrolled roadmap" bullet requires a `--from-stage` re-run:
  ```
  that file is non-canonical until its owning stage is re-run with `--from-stage`, which an operator must do before the evidence becomes citable.

  ```
  The fix is always to write the evidence row in exact rendered form (the route `--revise-feedback` already requires via `RenderCanonicalMismatch`), never to re-run the owning stage with `--from-stage` to "fix" canonicity
  ```
  Case 9 is the better-reasoned side, for two reasons. First, it names the hazard: a `--from-stage` run over an open feedback row is a backend call, and `roadmap.py:_newly_settled_decision_ids` shows that run may settle the decision itself, which leaves settlement refusing as case 3. Second, it matches the existing render-canonical contract in `ROADMAP_FORMAT.md`, which says the exact rendered feedback comment is canonical and "a hand-edited version is not". Because the plan contradicts itself, step 7's docs could tell operators to take the path that case 9 says defeats the settlement.

title: Step 6's acceptance criteria states that an incomplete or repeated flag triple "returns status 2 with `refusal` reported
body: Step 6's acceptance criteria states that an incomplete or repeated flag triple "returns status 2 with `refusal` reported as `mode-rejected` (or `confirmation-required` when the confirm flag alone is the one missing, matching the runner's own precedence)." This undersells the actual precedence rule the same detail file quotes correctly elsewhere: step 4's run order checks `confirmation is not True → confirmation-required` unconditionally, before checking `mode_rejected`, and step 6's own Input section states this must be preserved by "passing both values straight through and never short-circuiting one in front of the other." So `confirmation-required` actually fires whenever the confirm flag is absent, *regardless* of whether a decision or evidence selector is also missing at the same time — not only when confirm is the sole missing piece. For example, omitting both `--confirm-decision-settlement` and `--settle-decision` together still yields `confirmation-required`, not `mode-rejected`, contradicting a literal reading of "when the confirm flag alone is the one missing." No test in step 6 pins the actual resulting refusal string for a combined-missing-flags case: `test_decision_settlement_incomplete_or_repeated_triple_reaches_only_settlement_preflight` only asserts that `mode_rejected=True` was computed and forwarded to a *stubbed* runner, never the real refusal value a genuine run order would produce. The underlying precedence rule is separately and correctly pinned by step 4's own runner tests, so this is a documentation-only imprecision, not a functional gap.
suggested_action: Reword step 6's acceptance-criteria parenthetical to state the actual rule precisely (confirmation-required fires whenever the confirm flag is absent, independent of what else is missing or repeated), and add one CLI-level dispatch test using the real runner (or a precedence-aware stub) that exercises a combined "confirm and one selector both missing" input to pin the resulting refusal string end to end.

title: Acceptance criterion 4 and step 6 (`Render step 4's shared stack printout on the proposal output, the structural decisio
body:
Acceptance criterion 4 and step 6 (`Render step 4's shared stack printout on the proposal output, the structural decision …`) never say which outputs show the stack for which kinds of candidate. Two readers can ship different output. The gap has three parts:
  - (a) Criterion 4 names fewer surfaces than the Architecture and step 6. The Architecture and step 6 include the answered route's `--review-candidate` and `--answer-question` output, but no criterion locks those in.
    ```
    Every approve/confirm surface, and the proposal output, presents every unpromoted hop from the candidate's recorded root to the candidate, together with the cumulative diff, and the promote-review-seal output lists the same hops after the head has moved.
    ```
    (Acceptance criteria, bullet 4.)
    ```
    The whole stack is presented on every surface that asks for or confirms an approval: the structural decision, the answered route's review, answer, and promote surfaces, and the proposal output.
    ```
    (Architecture, owner decision 2.)
  - (b) The answered route only ever sees stacks with no structural hop, since step 2 makes it refuse a structural stack. The plan never says whether those stacks, or a single-hop presentation-only proposal, print the stack. `tests/cli/test_roadmap_cmd.py::test_presentation_candidate_keeps_the_existing_proposal_output` pins today's single-hop proposal output for a presentation-only candidate. Read literally, "presents every unpromoted hop" and that test disagree, and the plan does not choose.
  - (c) Selector-era candidates have no "recorded root". Their evidence and admission both carry `root_version_id` as None (`plan_tool/roadmap_candidate_run.py`, "selector-era candidate evidence cannot claim batch route facts"). They are still reviewed and promoted through `--review-candidate`, `--answer-question` and `--promote-review-seal`, through the non-batch branch of `_load_complete_sealed_candidate`. Step 4's view and step 6's promote output have no defined input for them. A view builder that raises on a missing root would fail after the head has already moved.
suggested_action: State one rule of which outputs print the whole-stack printout, for which candidate kinds, and align Architecture decision 2, step 6, acceptance criterion 4 and Testing to it. Cover batch-lineage candidates (including stacks with no structural hop) and selector-era and route-less candidates, which are a live legacy contract and keep their current output. Name the pinned presentation-only proposal-output test as one to rewrite.

title: Step 1 (`Add one stack-route derivation beside source_ancestry_to_root ...`) handles only an absent route, so a hop whos
body:
Step 1 (`Add one stack-route derivation beside source_ancestry_to_root ...`) handles only an absent route, so a hop whose evidence cannot be read has no stated outcome. Steps 2 and 3 (the guards and the recovery predicate) all consume that answer. The Architecture "Stack route" bullet says "The derivation reads the stored value and never reads meaning into an absent one", but it never separates "evidence present, no route" (a legacy or answered-replacement hop) from "evidence missing or fails validation". At HEAD, `load_stored_candidate_proposal` checks the ancestry only at the version-record level through `source_ancestry_to_root`, and never loads an ancestor's own evidence. The missing-ancestor-evidence case therefore appears only in the new derivation. `roadmap_revision_publish.py:_selected_promotion_is_structural` turns any `ValueError` into `None` (`CandidateProposalError` is a `ValueError`). It then refuses only because `_is_legacy_selector_only_promotion` returns False when the top candidate's evidence file exists. A derivation that reads a missing hop as "no structural hop" would let a promotion finish, or recovery complete, without its seed effect. That is the Risks entry "Recovery that computes the route differently from the writer can finish a promotion without its seed effect". The property, from Scope guardrails:

  ```
  Binary observable: every promotion whose ancestry from its recorded root contains a hop with a stored STRUCTURAL route is sealed as `structural-approval` on its top candidate after a matching confirm digest, and it journals the enrolled seed-state member. No other promotion carries a STRUCTURAL hop.
  ```
suggested_action: State once in the Stack route contract that a missing, non-candidate, or unvalidated hop makes the whole stack underivable and that steps 2 and 3 refuse it, separate from an absent stored route, which contributes nothing. Add that refusal to the Testing section and the acceptance criteria.

body: Step 3 (`Make the promotion boundary and the recovery predicate stack-aware ...`) promises a refusal its design cannot deliver with the review guards stubbed out.   ```
  reviewer-sealed. The dedicated settlement sentinel and `PendingGeneration`
  kind exist precisely so nothing needs to be faked.
  ```

An implementer must either build a fake capsule receipt to reuse that function, which is the synthetic provenance the Risk forbids, or invent a meaning the plan never states. The Testing section checks only the sentinel. The stored version record is the one lasting link between an accepted head and what produced it, so `content_identity` is also the natural place for a settlement version to name its receipt. Sites: Architecture "Enrolled roadmap" bullet, step 5 title, Risks "Synthetic provenance", and the Testing sentence on `review_lineage_identity`.
suggested_action: State that a settlement version's `content_identity` is a settlement-owned identity, for example one computed over the predecessor version id, artifact key, decision id, and cited feedback id/digest, or the receipt's identity. title: Step 1 (`Add one stack-route derivation beside source_ancestry_to_root ...`) and step 4 (`Build the whole-stack view, it
body:
Step 1 (`Add one stack-route derivation beside source_ancestry_to_root ...`) and step 4 (`Build the whole-stack view, its digest, and its one shared printout`) never say whether the recorded root is itself a hop, and the code makes the wrong reading easy. The Architecture "Stack route" sentence says "any hop from the candidate's recorded root to the candidate". `source_ancestry_to_root` returns the ids "through the root, inclusive", and step 1 sits "beside" it. The root is not always a candidate whose route can be read. It can be an enrolled root (`load_stored_candidate_proposal` raises for a non-candidate version). It can be a previously promoted structural candidate (its stored route is STRUCTURAL). It can be a head published by decision settlement (`roadmap_decision_settlement_enrolled.py` creates it with `create_candidate_version` and stores no candidate evidence). Counting the root as a hop has two effects:
  - A candidate rooted at an enrolled root or a settlement head becomes underivable, because the plan says a hop that "is not a stored candidate" is underivable. Every guard then refuses it.
  - After any structural promotion, every later presentation-only stack reads as structural. It is forced through `--decide-candidate` and refused on the answered route.

  Testing and the acceptance criterion "Legacy candidates without a route, and all-presentation stacks, keep their current routes" do not pin a stack rooted at a promoted structural candidate or a settlement head, so the green suite would not catch this. Sites: Architecture "Stack route"; step 1; step 4 (the hop list and the base of the cumulative diff); Testing; the acceptance criteria listed above; the Risks entry on the derivation being shared.
suggested_action: Define the hops as the unpromoted candidates strictly above the recorded root, so the root's own stored route (or lack of one) is never read and never loaded as a hop. Add the three root kinds (enrolled root, previously promoted structural candidate, settlement-published head) as asserted carve-outs in Testing and the acceptance criteria.

body: Step 2's classifier (`classify_arm_clustering`) always calls `AuditInputSnapshot.capture(plan_path, repo_root)` with no `detail_grade` argument, so it always captures the run-grade detail bundle by default — even though `cmd_convergence` (step 4) already accepts and threads a `--grade` flag (`args.grade`, run or jira) into `_current_audit_stage` for the same plan in the same command.
